claims.text: Spark plasma sintering can produce a large-scale reaction and stable composite microstructure in systems combining refractory high-entropy alloy powders with copper.
The initial material is a homogeneous powder mixture of refractory high-entropy alloy constituents and copper.
The SPS process uses rapid heating, a short dwell time, high pressure, and an inert atmosphere.
Optimized temperature and pressure enable fast reaction kinetics while limiting excessive elemental diffusion.
An inert atmosphere avoids oxidation during SPS.
Rapid SPS forms fine interfacial reaction layers or diffusion barriers.
Fine interfacial reaction layers or diffusion barriers maintain phase separation and prevent large-scale segregation.
Rapid sintering minimizes the time available for detrimental elemental diffusion.
The positive heat of mixing drives detrimental diffusion between the constituents.
Restricting diffusion promotes a controlled in-situ reaction that locks in a stable composite microstructure.
SPS produces a uniform distribution of copper within a refractory matrix.
The SPS composite has greater mechanical strength than conventionally sintered samples.
The SPS composite has greater irradiation resistance than conventionally sintered samples.
The SPS composite has greater thermal stability than conventionally sintered samples.
Slower conventional sintering permits extensive diffusion that leads to segregation and unstable microstructures in this system.
Successful formation of the proposed composite depends on careful optimization of SPS heating rate, dwell time, and pressure.
Uniform SPS processing may be difficult to scale to very large components because of thermal gradients.
Extreme disparities in elemental diffusivities may prevent the method from producing the proposed stable microstructure.
